seo.title: St Patrick: the British slave who went back to Ireland
seo.description: Saint Patrick in his own words: taken as a slave at sixteen, called back by a dream, and the truth about the snakes, the shamrock and the green.

band.lede: A British boy taken as a slave, who went back to the land of his captors and never left it.

who: Patrick was a Roman Briton, not an Irishman. Irish raiders seized him at sixteen, and he spent six years as a slave, herding flocks. He escaped home, then went back as a bishop and stayed in Ireland for good. Two short Latin writings of his survive. He died in 461, or about 493.

tidbits.text: The Irish called him Cothraige. Tírechán, in the 600s, took it to mean a slave in “the houses of four magicians”.

cite.text: White, notes on the Confession, chapter 1 (1920)

tidbits.text: Bede, the great English historian of the 700s, never names him in his *Ecclesiastical History*. He records only Palladius, sent to the Irish in 431.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 13, with Sellar's note (1907)

tidbits.text: A chief gave him a bronze pot, then took it back. Both times, says Muirchú, Patrick said only “Grazacham”, his Latin {la|gratias agamus}, meaning let us give thanks. The chief gave it back, with the hill of Armagh.

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapter 24, with White's note on the Confession, chapter 19

tidbits.text: The druids foretold his coming, says Muirchú: “Adze-head will come With his crook-headed staff”. The adze-head was the shaven head of a monk.

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapter 10, with White's notes (1920)

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 389, by Bury's reckoning, near a place he calls **Bannavem Taberniae**, in Roman Britain. No one knows where it was. Guesses run from **Dumbarton** in Scotland to the **Severn**.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His father **Calpurnius** was a deacon and a town councillor. His grandfather **Potitus** was a priest. Muirchú names his mother **Concessa**.

facts.label: Captured
facts.text: At about 16, by Irish raiders, from the family's small farm. A slave in Ireland for **six years**.

facts.label: Trained
facts.text: Somewhere in **Gaul**, most likely. Tírechán says the island monastery of **Lérins**, Muirchú says **Auxerre**. He never says.

facts.label: Bishop in
facts.text: **Ireland**, where he stayed until he died. Tradition makes **Armagh** his chief church.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: On **17 March**, in **461** or about **493**, most likely at **Saul** in County Down.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At **Downpatrick**, says Muirchú. Armagh and Glastonbury once claimed his grave too.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Sucat**, or Sochet, at home. **Cothraige** in Irish. The **Apostle of Ireland**. The **Enlightener of Ireland** in the Orthodox churches.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: The *Confession*, in old age, and a **letter** to the soldiers of a British king, **Coroticus**. Both in Latin.

facts.label: His Latin
facts.text: Rough, and he knew it. His schooling stopped when he was taken. He called Latin “a tongue not my own”.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A bishop with a crozier. From the later legends, a shamrock in his hand and snakes at his feet.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.

west.text: **Catholic**: an optional memorial in the general calendar, and a solemnity in **Ireland**. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The **Orthodox** churches that keep him, as the **OCA** does: “Enlightener of Ireland”.
Churches on the old calendar, which keep 17 March on this day.

feasts.note: Why one day? He lived long before East and West split, and both keep 17 March. Early copies of the martyrology called Jerome's, and Bede's, mark it as the day he was laid to rest, notes Rome's calendar of 1969. Rome itself added his feast to its calendar only in 1631. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later.

traits.title: ashamed of his Latin
traits.text: His schooling stopped when he was taken, and he never caught up. Others had studied from childhood. He had not. “For my speech and language is translated into a tongue not my own”, he wrote. “And so to-day I blush and am exceedingly afraid to lay bare my lack of education”.

traits.title: given to prayer
traits.text: As a slave on the hills he prayed through the day and much of the night. “And before daybreak I used to be roused to prayer, in snow, in frost, in rain; and I felt no hurt”. He felt no hurt, he says, because the spirit burned in him then.

traits.title: clean-handed
traits.text: Devout women laid their jewellery on the altar for him. He gave it back, and they were offended. He would not let anyone say he had profited from a baptism or an ordination. His challenge: “if I demanded from one of them even the price of my shoe; tell it against me and I shall restore you more.”

traits.title: stubborn in his calling
traits.text: His family wept and offered gifts to keep him home. His elders were against it too. He went anyway: “And I displeased them, and also, against my wish, not a few of my elders; but, God being my guide, in no way did I consent or yield to them.”

traits.title: cut deep by a friend
traits.text: The man who betrayed his secret was his closest friend. That still hurt as he wrote: “But rather I am grieved for my dearest friend that we should have merited to hear such an answer as that; a man to whom I had even entrusted my soul!”

traits.title: unafraid
traits.text: He lived among people who could kill him on any day, and said so plainly: “for daily I expect either slaughter, or to be defrauded, or reduced to slavery, or an unfair attack of some kind.” Then: “But none of these things move me”.

traits.title: tender to his captors' people
traits.text: He knew how strange his love for the Irish was. They had enslaved him and ruined his father's house. He could only credit God with it: “Is it from me that springs that godly compassion which I exercise towards that nation who once took me captive, and made havoc of the menservants and maidservants of my father's house?”

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapter 10

traits.title: fierce for his flock
traits.text: When British soldiers killed and carried off his converts, he called them “fellow-citizens of demons because of their evil deeds”. He told Christians to shun them: “It is not right to pay court to such men, nor to take food or drink with them”.

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapters 2 and 7

said.lede: The first *Lives* came two centuries after him. Since then he has been praised, doubted and argued over, sometimes by the same people.

quotes.q: …he used to sign himself with the sign of the cross a hundred times every hour of the day and night. And whenever he saw a cross, he would alight from his car, and turn aside there to pray.
quotes.who: Muirchú, in the oldest *Life* of Patrick, before 700

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 2, chapter 1, tr. White (1920)

quotes.q: …the birthday of St. Patrick, bishop and confessor, who was the first to preach Christ in that country, and became illustrious by great miracles and virtues.
quotes.who: The *Roman Martyrology*, 1916 edition, its entry for Ireland on 17 March

quotes.q: I incline to the opinion that they are the issue of an age subsequent to that of Ireland's Saint.
quotes.who: James O'Leary, a priest, on the *Confession* and the letter. He printed them in his book of 1874 all the same.

cite.text: James O'Leary, The Most Ancient Lives of Saint Patrick, preface

quotes.q: …it would perhaps be more correct to style him, with the ‘Annals of Ulster’ and the poet Ninnine, ‘Chief Apostle of Ireland.’
quotes.who: Thomas Olden, in the *Dictionary of National Biography*, 1895. His work did not reach the whole island, Olden noted.

quotes.q: His was evidently an intensely spiritual nature, and in addition to the qualities which go to form a strong man of action he must have possessed an enthusiasm which enabled him to surmount all difficulties.
quotes.who: Edmund Crosby Quiggin, in the *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, 1911

quotes.q: These documents bear the stamp of genuineness upon them as plainly as does the Epistle of St. Paul to the Galatians or the Second to the Corinthians.
quotes.who: Newport J. D. White, his translator, 1920

cite.text: White, St. Patrick, His Writings and Life (1920), introduction

quotes.q: The moral and spiritual greatness of the man shines through every stumbling sentence of his ‘rustic’ Latin.
quotes.who: D. A. Binchy, the strictest of modern scholars of Patrick, as quoted by *Britannica*

moments.title: A deacon's son
moments.text: Patrick was born in Roman Britain, not in Ireland. His father Calpurnius was a deacon and a town councillor. His grandfather Potitus was a priest. The family had a small farm near a place he calls Bannavem Taberniae. No one now knows where that was. The boy was not religious. “I knew not the true God”, he admits.

cite.text: Confession, chapter 1; Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapter 10

moments.title: Taken by raiders
moments.text: Irish raiders fell on the farm and carried him off. He was one of “many thousands of persons” taken to Ireland that time. He saw it as a judgement: “because we departed away from God, and kept not His commandments, and were not obedient to our priests”.

moments.title: A hundred prayers a day
moments.text: He was set to herding flocks for one master. Alone on the hills, his faith woke up. “Love of God and the fear of Him increased more and more”, he wrote. He stayed out “even in the woods and on the mountain” to pray. Tradition names the mountain as Slemish, in County Antrim.

moments.title: “Lo, thy ship is ready”
moments.text: One night a voice told him he would soon go home. Soon after came another: “Lo, thy ship is ready.” The ship was about two hundred miles away, where he had never been. He ran from his master and reached it the day it sailed. The captain refused him: “On no account seek to go with us.” As Patrick walked away praying, a sailor shouted him back.

moments.title: Hunger on the road
moments.text: After three days at sea they landed, and walked for twenty-eight days through empty country. The food ran out. The captain turned on him: “How is this, O Christian? thou sayest that thy God is great and almighty; wherefore then canst thou not pray for us, for we are in danger of starvation?” Patrick told them to turn to God. Soon a herd of pigs crossed their path.

moments.title: The Voice of the Irish
moments.text: Home at last, his family begged him never to leave again. Then he dreamt of a man called Victoricus, coming from Ireland with “countless letters”. The first was headed “The Voice of the Irish”. As he read, he heard the people of the Wood of Foclut, by the western sea, calling him back. He woke “exceedingly broken in heart”.

moments.title: Doubted by his elders
moments.text: He does not say where he trained. He speaks of longing to see “the brethren” in Gaul again. A saying kept in the *Book of Armagh* has him travel through Gaul, Italy and the islands of the Tyrrhene Sea. Muirchú puts him with Bishop Germanus at Auxerre. His elders thought him unfit: “Why does this fellow thrust himself into danger amongst hostile people who know not God?”

cite.text: Confession, chapters 43 and 46; Sayings of Patrick; Muirchú, Book 1, chapter 6

moments.title: Bishop in Ireland
moments.text: He went back against his family's tears: “And many gifts were proffered me with weeping and tears.” In 431 Pope Celestine had sent a bishop, Palladius, to the Irish who already believed. Patrick's mission is traditionally dated to the next year. He calls himself simply “a bishop, appointed by God, in Ireland”.

cite.text: Confession, chapter 37; Letter, chapter 1; Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 13

moments.title: Thousands baptized
moments.text: He baptized “many thousands of persons” and ordained clergy everywhere. He went, he says, where no one had come “to baptize, or ordain clergy, or confirm the people”. He gave presents to kings and paid their sons to travel with him. He paid the judges “not less than the price of fifteen men”. Once a king's men seized him and put him in irons, meaning to kill him. He was free on the fourteenth day.

moments.title: Chieftains' daughters
moments.text: “Sons and daughters of Scottic chieftains are seen to become monks and virgins of Christ.” The Scots here are the Irish. One noble young woman came back a few days after her baptism: an angel had told her to give her life to God. Six days later she did. Many did so against their fathers' will. Women held as slaves had it hardest: “they constantly endure even unto terrors and threats.”

moments.title: The massacre
moments.text: Soldiers of Coroticus, a British king, raided his new converts the day after their baptism. The oil was “still fragrant on their foreheads” when they were cut down. Others were carried off to be sold. Patrick sent a priest to ask for the captives. “They jeered at them.” So he wrote an open letter, to be read out before the king himself.

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapters 2, 3 and 21

moments.title: Betrayed by his dearest friend
moments.text: His elders in Britain turned on him. They dug up a sin from his youth, from about the age of fifteen, which he had told his closest friend before he was even a deacon. He never says what it was. That same friend had once backed him: “Lo, thou art to be raised to the rank of bishop”. Now the friend shamed him in public. The *Confession* is Patrick's answer.

moments.title: Bound to Ireland
moments.text: He longed to visit his family in Britain and the brothers in Gaul. He would not go. “I am bound in the Spirit”, he wrote, and feared to lose the work he had begun. He stayed in Ireland to the end, and wrote his *Confession* there “before I die”.

extras.title: When did he live?
extras.lede: Even his century is argued over. The old annals give more than one year for his death, and each has its defenders.

items.title: Died 461
items.text: The *Annals of Ulster* note, at 461, that some record his death then. The historian J. B. Bury worked out 389 to 461, and his translator White agreed. Rome's own calendar of 1969 gives 461. So do the Episcopal Church and the ELCA.
items.quote: …a man who lived between a.d. 389 and a.d. 461, the dates of St. Patrick's birth and death according to the most recent calculations.

cite.text: White, introduction (1920); The Annals of Ulster, at 461, in the CELT translation; Calendarium Romanum (1969); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; ELCA

items.title: Died 493
items.text: The same annals, at 493, have him die on 17 March in his hundred and twentieth year, sixty years after he came to Ireland. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1911 followed this date, with his birth in 387. The OCA gives 461, “some say 492”. Olden, in 1895, thought 493 rested only on the idea of sixty years' labour from 432. *Britannica* places his mission in the second half of the 400s: his letter still calls the Franks heathen, so it was written before their baptism in 496.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), “St. Patrick”; The Annals of Ulster, at 493; OCA, 17 March; Dictionary of National Biography (1895); Britannica

items.title: Palladius, and two Patricks?
items.text: Pope Celestine sent Palladius to the Irish in 431. Muirchú says he failed and soon died in Britain. The annals also record the death of an elder Patrick in 457. So some have wondered if two men's stories were woven into one. Heinrich Zimmer argued that Palladius and Patrick were the same man. White called that notion refuted. Thomas Olden thought the confusion was medieval:
items.quote: …the belief that two persons were confused together—one the simple missionary of the ‘Confession,’ the other the great thaumaturge of whom so many marvels were told.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 13; Muirchú, Book 1, chapter 8; The Annals of Ulster, at 457; Britannica (1911); White (1920); Dictionary of National Biography (1895)

extras.title: The Breastplate: is it his?
extras.lede: The best-loved prayer under his name is an Irish hymn called the *Lorica*, or Breastplate. In Irish it is the Deer's Cry. Whether he wrote it is argued. Here are both sides.

items.title: What it is
items.text: A lorica was a prayer for protection, worn like armour. This one survives in manuscripts from the 1000s on. It calls on the Trinity, on Christ's life, on the angels and on the powers of creation. It asks for help against “spells of women and smiths and druids”. Cecil Frances Alexander turned it into the English hymn “I bind unto myself today”, printed in 1889.
items.quote: I arise to-day: in the might of Heaven; brightness of Sun; whiteness of Snow; splendour of Fire; speed of Lightning; swiftness of Wind; depth of Sea; stability of Earth; firmness of Rock.

cite.text: The Lorica, stanza 4, tr. Atkinson, in White (1920); Hymnary.org

items.title: For: “Patrick made this hymn”
items.text: An old Irish preface says so, and gives the day: he sang it on the road to Tara, when King Loegaire laid an ambush. His men were seen as wild deer, and so it got its name. The *Book of Armagh*, written about 807, bids the churches always sing his Irish canticle, {la|canticum eius Scotticum}. White saw no reason to doubt it. Its editor Robert Atkinson thought its odd grammar more likely old than faked. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1911 called it “now universally accepted as genuine”.
items.quote: Patrick made this hymn; in the time of Loegaire macNeill it was made, and the cause of its composition was for the protection of himself and his monks against the deadly enemies that lay in ambush for the clerics.

cite.text: Preface to the Lorica, tr. Atkinson, in White (1920); Catholic Encyclopedia (1911)

items.title: Against: later than Patrick
items.text: Many scholars now date it after his time. Muirchú tells the story of the deer at Tara but says nothing of a hymn. White granted that tying the name Deer's Cry to that story may be “due to a false derivation of the name in later times”. The Episcopal Church's book of saints says the hymn was probably not his, but still expresses “his faith and zeal”.
items.quote: …was probably not written by him, dating most probably from the eighth century rather than from the fifth…

cite.text: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 17 March; White, introduction to the Lorica (1920)

items.title: “Christ with me”
items.text: Whoever wrote it, its seventh stanza is among the best-known prayers of the Irish Church. In 1839 the antiquary George Petrie found part of it still said by country people “usually at bed-time”. Eleanor Hull suspected they were saying the older charms it grew from.
items.quote: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ under me, Christ over me, Christ to right of me, Christ to left of me, Christ in lying down, Christ in sitting, Christ in rising up.

cite.text: The Lorica, stanza 7, tr. Atkinson; Petrie (1839), as quoted by White (1920)

miracles.lede: In his own writings Patrick works no wonders. He tells of answered prayer, voices in the night and dreams. The marvels arrive with the writers who came after him: Tírechán about 670, Muirchú before 700, and Jocelin in the late 1100s. Muirchú was frank about his sources:

pledge.q: My skill is small; my authorities are uncertain [or, anonymous]; my memory is treacherous; my intelligence is worn out; my style is poor; yet the feeling of my love is most pious.

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, preface, tr. White (1920)

feature.title: wonders of his first Easter, as Muirchú tells it

items.title: The fire
items.text: The High King Loegaire held a pagan feast at Tara that night. No one might light a fire before the king's own. Patrick kept Easter on the great plain, in sight of Tara, and lit his Easter fire first. Muirchú places it at a spot called the Graves of the Men of Fecc. Later tellers put it on the hill of Slane.
items.quote: kindled a divine fire, very bright and blessed, which as it shone forth at night, was seen by almost all the dwellers in the plain
items.witness: The king's magicians: “unless it be put out on this night on which it has been lighted up, it will not be put out for ever.”

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapters 13 to 15; Britannica (1911)

items.title: Eight stags and a fawn
items.text: The king summoned him, pretending peace, and meant to kill him. Patrick blessed his eight men and a boy in the name of Jesus Christ and walked towards the king. The king counted them as they came, and then they were gone.
items.quote: but the heathen folk saw nought but eight stags and a fawn going as it were to the wilderness
items.witness: Loegaire and the few with him, who went back to Tara at dawn.

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapter 18

items.title: Snow on the plain
items.text: At the king's feast a magician challenged him. He brought snow down on the whole plain, waist deep, but could not take it away. Patrick told him, “Thou art able to do evil, but not good; I am not of that sort.” Then Patrick blessed the plain.
items.quote: and the snow vanished quicker than a word could be uttered, without any rain or cloud or wind
items.witness: The feast. The contest ended in a trial by fire, and the king gave in: “It is better for me to believe than to die.”

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapters 20 and 21

note.text: Muirchú tells that night as a new Book of Daniel. Tara is “their Babylon” and Loegaire a Nebuchadnezzar. The 1911 *Britannica* read it as a story told “in picturesque fashion”, of a real clash with the king's power.

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapter 15; Britannica (1911)

more.title: Pigs in the empty land
more.text: His own story, told as answered prayer. The starving sailors had mocked his God. He told them to turn to Him, and it came about, he says, “by the help of God”. They stayed two nights and ate their fill, and thanked God.
more.quote: Lo, a herd of swine appeared in the way before our eyes

more.title: The sun at night
more.text: Also his own. That same night Satan fell on him in his sleep “as it were a huge rock”, and he could not move. He cried out “Helias”, perhaps meaning Elijah, perhaps the sun, Helios. He believed Christ had helped him.
more.quote: lo, the splendour of that sun fell upon me, and straightway shook all weight from off me

more.title: The fawn at Armagh
more.text: When Daire gave him the hill of Armagh, they found a doe and her fawn where the altar would stand. His men wanted to kill the fawn. Patrick would not allow it.
more.quote: the Saint himself took the fawn and carried it on his shoulders. And the hind followed him, like a gentle and tame sheep

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapter 24

more.title: A king turned fox
more.text: Muirchú's ending for Coroticus, who mocked Patrick's letter. Patrick prayed that God would banish him from this world and the next. In the middle of his court the king changed shape and was never seen again.
more.quote: took on the spot the form of a little fox

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 1, chapter 29

more.title: Twelve nights without dark
more.text: When he died, says Muirchú, the nights of mourning stayed light for twelve days. The people of Ulster said the nights were never so dark again that year.
more.quote: Because on the day of his death there was no night

cite.text: Muirchú, Life of Patrick, Book 2, chapter 8

more.title: A later legend: 33 raised
more.text: Jocelin, a monk of Furness, wrote his *Life* in the late 1100s. It holds the snakes, and much more. He credits Patrick with 350 bishops, 700 churches, and the dead brought back:
more.quote: Thirty and three dead men, some of whom had many years been buried, did this great reviver raise from the dead

cite.text: Jocelin, Life and Acts of St. Patrick, chapters 185 and 186, tr. Edmund L. Swift (1809)

doubt.title: Doubted, then and now
doubt.text: The 1911 *Britannica* trusted Muirchú on Patrick's early years, but once the story reaches Ireland, it wrote, “Muirchu's narrative becomes full of the mythical element.” White thought the real Patrick of the writings was “quite other” than “the somewhat vindictive saint who was Muirchu's hero”. James O'Leary, who printed the old *Lives* in 1874, left the verdict to his readers: “Their narratives may be pronounced fables, or legends, or inventions, or superstitions, or histories.”

cites.text: O'Leary, The Most Ancient Lives of Saint Patrick, preface

words.note: Two short writings are surely his: the *Confession*, written in old age, and an open letter to the soldiers of a British king. Both are in rough Latin. They are quoted here in Newport J. D. White's translation of 1920.

feature.kicker: The dream that called him back
feature.q: We beseech thee, holy youth, to come and walk among us once more.
feature.ctx: Home in Britain, he dreamt of a letter from Ireland headed “The Voice of the Irish”. As he read it, he heard them cry out “as with one mouth”. His Latin word for Ireland was {la|Hiberio}.

quotes.q: I, Patrick the sinner, am the most illiterate and the least of all the faithful, and contemptible in the eyes of very many.
Whence came to me this wisdom, which was not in me, I who neither knew the number of my days, nor cared for God?
It was not any grace in me, but God Who overcometh in me.
quotes.who: On why he went, against everyone.

quotes.q: Moreover, as regards those heathen amongst whom I dwell, I have kept faith with them, and will keep it.
Sufficient to me is the honour which is not seen as yet, but is believed on in the heart.
quotes.who: To those who thought he wanted honour.

quotes.q: Behold, we are witnesses that the Gospel has been preached to the limit beyond which no man dwells.
quotes.who: Ireland, to him, was the edge of the world.

quotes.q: We, on the other hand, who believe in and worship the true sun, Christ — Who will never perish
quotes.who: Against the sun worship he saw around him.

quotes.q: It is in their eyes a disgraceful thing that we were born in Ireland.
quotes.who: Of the British raiders who despised his Irish converts.

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapter 16

quotes.q: Thanks be to God, it was as baptized believers that ye departed from the world to Paradise. I can see you.
quotes.who: To the converts who were killed.

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapter 17

quotes.q: I had the fear of God as the guide of my journey through Gaul and Italy and, moreover, in the islands which are in the Tyrrhene Sea.
quotes.who: One of three sayings of his kept in the *Book of Armagh*.

myths.truth: He was a Roman Briton, and says so: “I was freeborn according to the flesh; I am born of a father who was a decurion”, a Roman town councillor. Muirchú agreed he “was of the British race and born in Britain”. Ireland was the land of his captivity, and then of his choice.

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, chapter 10; Muirchú, Book 1, chapter 1

myths.claim: He drove the snakes out of Ireland.
myths.truth: Ireland had no snakes to drive. Bede noted it in 731, and never linked it to Patrick: “No reptiles are found there, and no snake can live there”. The story is told by Jocelin, in the late 1100s: Patrick drove every poisonous creature onto Croagh Patrick and “by the power of his word he drove the whole pestilent swarm from the precipice of the mountain headlong into the ocean.” *Britannica* notes that scientists say “Ireland has never had snakes”. The OCA agrees many see “no historical basis” in it.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 1; Jocelin, chapter 170, tr. Swift (1809); Britannica; OCA, 17 March

myths.claim: He taught the Trinity with a shamrock.
myths.truth: It is not in his writings or in any of the early *Lives*. The first writer known to record it is the botanist Caleb Threlkeld, in 1726. He wrote that the plant “is worn by the People in their Hats upon the 17. Day of March yearly”, and called the Trinity story “a Current Tradition”. The OCA tells it as fact. *The Spectator* judged the tradition “impossible to date”, and said it “could indeed be founded on reality”.

cite.text: Threlkeld, Synopsis Stirpium Hibernicarum (1726; 1727 printing); OCA, 17 March; The Spectator

myths.truth: It was once blue. The earliest pictures of him, notes *Smithsonian* magazine, “show him clothed in blue garments, not green”. When George III founded the Order of St Patrick, its colour was a sky blue, called St Patrick's blue. Green took over from the late 1700s, as a colour of Irish identity and rebellion.

cite.text: Smithsonian magazine, on St Patrick's blue

myths.truth: There were Christians before him. In 431, says Bede, following Prosper, Palladius “was sent by Celestinus, the Roman pontiff, to the Scots that believed in Christ, to be their first bishop”. Patrick claims only to have gone further, to places “where never had any one come to baptize”. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* still called him “the first to preach Christ in that country”.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 13; Confession, chapter 51; Roman Martyrology (1916), 17 March

myths.truth: It is the day he died. The old martyrology does call 17 March his “birthday”, but in its own words a saint's birthday is “the day on which a Saint enters heaven”. Muirchú dates his death to “the 17th day of March”.

That is Moses's age, and the likeness was the point. Muirchú says he died “when the 120 years of his whole life had been completed”. An old British history spells it out: “In four points Patrick was like unto Moses”, the third being “because he passed 120 years in the present life”. Bury's dates make him about 72 when he died.

cite.text: Muirchú, Book 2, chapter 7; Historia Brittonum, as quoted by White (1920); Deuteronomy 34:7

circle.name: Martin of Tours
circle.text: Later tradition tied them together. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* made his mother Concessa “a near relative” of Martin. Later *Lives* sent Patrick to study at Tours, and Thomas Olden believed it: “without doubt was the master under whom Patrick studied”. Patrick never mentions him. On Bury's dates, Martin died when Patrick was about eight.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1911); Dictionary of National Biography (1895)

circle.name: Calpurnius
circle.text: His father: a deacon, and a decurion, a member of a Roman town council. He owned the small farm where his son was seized.

circle.name: Potitus
circle.text: His grandfather, a priest. White notes a married clergy raised no scandal then.

circle.name: Victoricus
circle.text: The man in the dream who brought the letter from Ireland. Muirchú made him an angel who had spoken to Patrick in his slavery.

circle.name: His dearest friend
circle.text: Unnamed. He heard Patrick's secret, backed him for bishop, then shamed him in public. White wondered if he was Germanus himself.

circle.name: Coroticus
circle.text: A British king, most likely of Strathclyde, ruling from the Rock of Dumbarton. His soldiers killed and enslaved Patrick's converts.

cite.text: Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus; White, introduction to the Letter (1920)

circle.name: Miliucc
circle.text: His master in slavery, by Muirchú's account. When Patrick came back to pay his ransom, Miliucc burned himself in his house rather than face his old slave.

circle.name: Loegaire
circle.text: High King at Tara, son of Niall. In Muirchú, the king of the Easter fire, who believed at last, grudgingly.

circle.name: Dichu
circle.text: His first convert, by Muirchú's account. He meant to kill the strangers, until he saw Patrick's face. His barn became the church at Saul, from the Irish for barn.

circle.name: Palladius
circle.text: Sent by Pope Celestine in 431 as the first bishop of the Irish believers. Muirchú says the Irish would not hear him, and he died in Britain.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapter 13; Muirchú, Book 1, chapter 8

circle.name: Germanus of Auxerre
circle.text: Bishop of Auxerre, in Gaul. Muirchú says Patrick studied with him for many years. Patrick never names him.

circle.name: Benignus
circle.text: Benen, his young companion: the fawn of the Deer's Cry. He followed Patrick at Armagh, says the 1911 *Britannica*.

cite.text: Preface to the Lorica, in White (1920); Britannica (1911)

circle.name: Tassach
circle.text: The bishop who gave him the last Sacrament, as he was dying.

death.big: He died in Ireland on 17 March, in 461 or about 493, most likely at Saul in County Down.
paras: His own writings end with the *Confession*, in old age. He expected a violent death, and hoped to share it with his converts. How he died we know only from later writers.

Muirchú says an angel told him death was near. He set out for Armagh, “which he loved beyond all other places”. On the way an angel stopped him and sent him back to Saul. There Bishop Tassach gave him the last Sacrament. White thought it “plain that he died at Saul”.

For the burial, Muirchú's angel had a plan: “Let two unbroken oxen be chosen, and let them go whithersoever they will, and in whatever place they lie down, let a church be built in honour of thy poor body.” The oxen stopped at Downpatrick. Two peoples nearly went to war over the body. Muirchú says the sea rose to keep them apart.

His grave was argued over for centuries: Saul, Downpatrick, Armagh and Glastonbury all claimed it. The *Annals of Ulster* say Colum Cille put his relics in a shrine sixty years after his death. In 1899 a granite slab was laid at his traditional grave at Downpatrick.

later.title: The later story
later.text: Later *Lives* gave him a grander deathbed. In the version the *Catholic Encyclopedia* retold in 1911, Brigid of Kildare came to him with her nuns, and he was buried in a shroud she had woven. Muirchú, the oldest *Life*, has no Brigid.

items.q: I pray Him to grant to me that I may shed my blood with those strangers and captives for His name's sake, even though I should lack burial itself

items.k: The last line of his Confession
items.q: And this is my confession before I die.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too. No pope ever canonised him: like the early saints, he was made one by the Church's memory.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: Ireland kept his day from early on, and the oldest martyrologies mark it. Rome added it to the calendar of the whole Western Church in 1631.

Thomas Olden, writing in 1895, put it bluntly: “he was never canonised at Rome, and his acceptance as a saint is the outcome of popular tradition.” That is true of nearly every saint of his age. Formal canonisation came centuries later.
He lived before the split between East and West, so the Orthodox can claim him too. The OCA keeps him on 17 March as the Enlightener of Ireland.

prayer.title: From his Confession
prayer.intro: In the middle of his defence, he stops arguing and gives thanks.
prayer.q: Hence therefore I render unwearied thanks to my God Who kept me faithful in the day of my temptation, so that to-day I can confidently offer to Him a sacrifice, as a living victim, my soul to Christ my Lord Who saved me out of all my troubles, so that I may say, Who am I, O Lord, or what is my calling, that Thou hast worked together with me with such divine power? so that to-day among the heathen I should steadfastly exult, and magnify Thy name wherever I may be; and that not only in prosperity, but also in troubles, so that whatever may happen to me, whether good or bad, I ought to receive it with an equal mind, and ever render thanks to God Who shewed me that I might trust Him endlessly.
